episode_title: The State of the Ukraine War

stories.topic: Zelensky: 'I want ammunition, not a ride'
stories.summary: Russia's intelligence expected a replay of Afghanistan: the West would buckle, the leadership would flee and the army would melt away. The Americans did offer Zelensky a flight out of Kyiv, as they had in Afghanistan. He refused, asked for ammunition instead, stayed and rallied his people. After that, the West turned around and committed to backing Ukraine.
stories.insight: Putin's whole plan rested on an assumption about will. One leader's refusal to run broke that assumption and changed the course of the war.
stories.quote: And Zelensky said, I don't want a ride, I want ammunition. Okay, that's just one of the most priceless moments in world history, where he said, No, this is my country. I will stand and fight.

stories.topic: How Europe beat Putin's energy blackmail
stories.summary: Putin bet that cutting gas to a Europe hooked on Russian pipelines would cause a deep recession and working-class anger. That anger, he hoped, would empower communists and Nazis and break the fragile centrist coalitions of Christian democrats and social democrats, a replay of the 1930s. Instead Europe tripled its work on renewables and imported LNG from all over the world. It built LNG terminals in six months when two to three years was thought necessary, and it subsidised poor households so nobody froze. Europe got through 2022 with difficulty but without a crisis.
stories.insight: Don't mistake the mild, self-effacing manner of advanced economies for weakness, because their intellectual, technological and financial depth is huge. Calling the bluff was also a strategic disaster for Russia: it lost its main gas buyer, and cheap gas sales to Europe were what its economy was built on.
stories.quote: Before the war, people believed that it takes two to three years to build an LNG terminal. They got LNG terminals done in six months.

stories.summary: Russia invaded Georgia on 8 August 2008 and nobody helped. In February 2014 Putin grabbed Crimea and nobody did anything. Putin concluded the West had no stomach for a fight. Ajay compares this to Hitler taking Austria and Czechoslovakia unopposed until he invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. Then Britain and France gave him an ultimatum and declared war. The 2022 invasion triggered a similar 'enough is enough' from the West.
stories.insight: Aggression that goes unpunished teaches the aggressor the wrong lesson, and appeasement tends to end abruptly, with the aggressor miscalculating.
stories.quote: And so he started getting comfortable that the West does not have a stomach for a fight.

stories.topic: The chess grandmasters who stood up to Putin
stories.summary: About 40 Russian chess grandmasters, essentially the country's top players, signed a letter protesting the invasion. Many had to leave Russia and now play for other federations. The lone holdout Amit names is Sergey Karyakin, whom he calls a coward. Ajay adds that Garry Kasparov, who had warned about Putin for years, was what woke him up. Before that he had seen Putin as just another Russian strongman; Kasparov showed him this was a man yearning for the USSR.
stories.insight: Always separate the Russian state from the Russian people. Many Russians have protested at real personal cost.
stories.quote: Many of them had to move out of the country. Some of them are now, you know, playing for other chess federations in tournaments around the world. All of them protested.

stories.summary: At 23, Peter McIndoe deliberately invented a conspiracy theory as a public experiment. His claim was that the US government had killed all the birds decades ago and replaced them with surveillance robots. The 'proof': birds sit on power lines to recharge, you never see baby pigeons because factories only make adults, and birds poop on people to track them. He kept up the charade for three years, driving around in a van handing out flyers, and many people believed it.
stories.insight: It is a delightful demonstration of how easily belief can be manufactured, and Amit brings it up while discussing drones as birds in a hostile sky.
stories.quote: Have you ever seen a baby pigeon? It's because only adult pigeons are created in the factories.

stories.topic: America built 100,000 tanks, then shut the factories
stories.summary: Until 1941 the American 'giant' was asleep. Then it started from scratch, built the world's biggest tank factories and turned out something like 100,000 tanks in roughly two years. By early 1944 field commanders were saying they didn't want any more, and factories started shutting down.
stories.insight: This is what 'arsenal of democracy' really meant. The American way of war was designed around that manufacturing might and a large population, so it doesn't transfer neatly to a smaller country like Ukraine.
stories.quote: And then the field commanders were saying we're sick of this. We don't want any more tanks.

stories.summary: With people and production to spare, the Americans were in a rush to launch Operation Torch in North Africa, then land in Sicily and on the beaches of Normandy. Churchill knew Britain's small population couldn't absorb heavy losses. He kept insisting they get it right and not let troops be mauled for almost nothing.
stories.insight: How many deaths a country can bear shapes its way of war. A smaller nation rationally fights more cautiously, which is the same logic behind Ukraine being frugal with its soldiers today.
stories.quote: And the Americans had to be held back consistently and I think history will judge Churchill very kindly for having had a lot of those strategic calls correctly.

stories.summary: After Operation Barbarossa in June 1941, German Army Groups North, Centre and South were spread along a very long front, heading for St Petersburg, Moscow and later Stalingrad and the Baku oil fields. Stalin had to decide whether to mass his forces for one breakthrough. Ajay counts him, with Lenin and Trotsky, among the sophisticated intellectuals of the era. Stalin knew the USSR had the bigger population and that, backed by American industry, it would outproduce Germany, something the Germans were naive about. So he counter-attacked everywhere to grind down German men and industry. Germany couldn't be strong everywhere, which is part of why it lost Stalingrad.
stories.insight: When the deeper resources are on your side, steady pressure everywhere can beat one concentrated thrust. You don't need to know in advance where the enemy will crack. This is the intuition behind Ukraine's current strategy.
stories.quote: You can't predict where it will break, but it'll break somewhere.

stories.topic: Bakhmut: losing a town to break Wagner
stories.summary: Bakhmut, a small town of about 70,000, was taken by Wagner. Simplistic war thinking says Ukraine should have retreated early, but cities are where you defend, so Ukraine fought a long fighting retreat. It lost the town, but inflicted such losses on Wagner that a rift opened with the Russian MOD, leading to the Wagner mutiny and knocking out a key Russian fighting formation. Like Stalingrad, Bakhmut has become a symbol. The MOD cannot afford to lose ground that Prigozhin and Utkin conquered, so Ukraine keeps pressing there, locking up Russian forces at a disproportionate cost.
stories.insight: In modern war, track the exchange rate of losses, not just territory. A place that has become a symbol can turn into a trap that drains the enemy.
stories.quote: By and large, Ukraine lost. But in the process of losing, they inflicted so much damage upon Wagner that it triggered off the mutiny by Wagner and it knocked out one important fighting formation on the Russian side.

stories.topic: Kherson and Kharkiv looked like stalemate, until they didn't
stories.summary: Before Ukraine's big 2022 gains, its attacks looked fruitless day after day. Underneath, Russia's ability to supply Kherson was collapsing. One day Russia simply left, and Ukraine retook the whole province without a fight. The Russian redeployment left a chunk near Kharkiv undefended, and Ukraine used spare forces to seize another 10,000 to 15,000 square kilometres.
stories.insight: An attritional phase can hide an imminent collapse. Judging a campaign by visible kilometres gained can badly mislead.
stories.quote: For some time, it's just like you're attacking, attacking every day, and nothing is happening. But under the hood, there was a lot going on.

stories.summary: Russia loudly claims it is fighting NATO. When Finland was neutral, Russia kept about 100 units on the Finnish border. Now that Finland has joined NATO, that force has fallen to about 20, one-fifth of its traditional size, because everything is being poured into Ukraine.
stories.insight: Watch what a state does, not what it says. The emptied border exposes the NATO-threat story as propaganda and shows how stretched Russia is.
stories.quote: Now Finland is a NATO member and Russia has 20 units on the Finland border.

stories.topic: Tezuka: 'I'm begging you, let me work'
stories.summary: Yoshihiro Tatsumi idolised Osamu Tezuka, then pioneered gekiga, a dark reaction against manga. Rather than resist, the master was taken by his admirer's form, championed it, and around 1970 wrote Ode to Kirihito in that spirit. Dying of stomach cancer in 1989, Tezuka kept drawing in hospital. When a nurse came to take his drawing equipment away, his last words were a plea to keep working. After his death his daughter found a drawer full of unfinished work.
stories.insight: A great master humble enough to learn from a young disciple, and a life of relentless devotion to craft right to the end.
stories.quote: And his last words were, I'm begging you, let me work.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The five-plus-hour Ukraine primer this episode updates. Amit opens with how his friend Gaurav Chintamani was blown away by it, and returns to it at the close.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a masterclass on the history of the conflict and the deep histories of Russia and Ukraine, and an essential counter to Russian propaganda.

recommendations.item: Russia, Ukraine, Foreign Policy (Episode 268 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane and Nitin Pai
recommendations.context: Recorded right when the war started. Amit mentions it while explaining Europe's dependence on Russian energy.
recommendations.reason: It covers Europe's disastrous choice to rely on Russian pipelines instead of building ports to diversify supply, the dependence Putin thought he could exploit.

recommendations.creator: Phillips Payson O'Brien
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation at the end of the episode.
recommendations.reason: A recent book offering new insights on the grunt on the ground versus the high economic strategy of the Second World War. Ajay has studied the subject all his life and still found it full of new knowledge.

recommendations.creator: Osamu Tezuka
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation, held up on camera as a well-thumbed copy. It is a circa-1970 medical thriller about a doctor investigating a contagious disease in a remote area that turns people into dog-like creatures, which he eventually catches himself.
recommendations.reason: One of the most powerful graphic novels he has read: an odyssey into the human condition and the moral decay circumstances can bring. Tezuka wrote it after being inspired by his admirer Tatsumi's gekiga movement.

recommendations.item: The Push Man and Other Stories
recommendations.creator: Yoshihiro Tatsumi
recommendations.context: A 1969 gekiga collection, later published in English by the Canadian house Drawn & Quarterly. Amit recounts 'Bedridden', in which a colleague sent to care for an injured worker's 'woman' finds a crippled sex slave and strangles the worker to become her ninth master.
recommendations.reason: Gekiga at its best: really dark urban stories that stare into the depths of the human soul and go where manga doesn't.

recommendations.creator: Yoshihiro Tatsumi
recommendations.context: Tatsumi's collection from a year after The Push Man. Amit describes 'My Beloved Monkey', in which a man who loses his arm releases his pet monkey into a zoo enclosure and watches the other monkeys tear it to shreds.
recommendations.reason: More bleak, unforgettable gekiga with endings you have to read for yourself.

recommendations.item: Birds Aren't Real? How a Conspiracy Takes Flight
recommendations.creator: Peter McIndoe
recommendations.context: Amit tells McIndoe's story when Ajay mentions enemy drones in the sky, and says he'll link a video of McIndoe explaining it.
recommendations.reason: A delightful first-hand account of how a deliberately invented conspiracy theory gets people to believe it.

recommendations.creator: Lawrence Freedman
recommendations.context: Amit calls it a great interview he had been reading.
recommendations.reason: Kofman captures what surprised everyone: the occupation was always expected to fail, but almost nobody expected the invasion itself to fail.

recommendations.item: The hard lessons from Ukraine's summer offensive
recommendations.creator: Christopher Miller and Ben Hall (Financial Times)
recommendations.context: Amit reads from this 'great piece' that Ajay had sent him.
recommendations.reason: It vividly describes the counteroffensive as 'a war of tree lines': small infantry groups advancing field by field under artillery and drones, slowly wearing down Russian defences.

recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: Invoked as the emblem of post-Cold War optimism when the Berlin Wall fell.
recommendations.reason: It captures the belief that history's arc had settled on liberal democracy, a belief the current wave of authoritarianism has shaken.

recommendations.context: Ajay suggests reading up on it while explaining Russia's fortified lines in Zaporizhzhia. At Kursk the Soviets built seven lines, and the Germans smashed through five before running out of juice.
recommendations.reason: Russia's defences today come straight from that Soviet playbook, and Ukraine has so far cut through only one to one-and-a-half of three or four lines.

recommendations.creator: DeepStateMap
recommendations.context: Ajay walks viewers through a map of Russian-held territory, from Crimea and the Kerch Bridge up to Kharkiv. The live map is linked in the show notes as 'The Map'.
recommendations.reason: The geography and logistics of the front only make sense when you can see them.

recommendations.item: The Problem (Washington Post on the Melitopol counteroffensive)
recommendations.creator: The Washington Post
recommendations.reason: Background on the challenge of Ukraine's push toward Melitopol and the Sea of Azov.

recommendations.item: Basic facts about the map (NYT interactive)
recommendations.creator: The New York Times
recommendations.reason: A visual primer on the counteroffensive's geography.

recommendations.creator: Lawrence Freedman
recommendations.reason: Takes on the disappointment that the counteroffensive hasn't produced a quick breakthrough.

recommendations.item: Perseverance and Adaptation: Ukraine's Counteroffensive at Three Months
recommendations.creator: Michael Kofman and Rob Lee (War on the Rocks)
recommendations.reason: A three-month assessment of how the counteroffensive is going.

recommendations.item: Stalemate, Zugzwang and a long Middle Game
recommendations.creator: Lawrence Freedman
recommendations.reason: Freedman's take on whether the war is a stalemate, in the same chess-flavoured terms the hosts use.

recommendations.item: Conflict in Ukraine: A timeline (2014 – present)
recommendations.creator: Nigel Walker (House of Commons Library)
recommendations.reason: A chronology of the conflict since Crimea in 2014.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay sees the defeat of Nazi Germany and the collapse of the USSR as the great humanising milestones of the 20th century, ushering in freedom and democracy worldwide. Putin wants to return to a world where big powers invade their neighbours. If he succeeds, Belarus and Poland come next, and China may make a play for Taiwan or India. With Trump, Xi, Putin and Erdogan in the picture, authoritarians prop each other up as Mussolini, Hitler and Imperial Japan once did. Just as the world couldn't ignore Spain in 1936, it can't ignore Ukraine now.
core_ideas.quote: liberal democracy is a fragile compact and we need to renew our vows every day.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay rejects the soft 'legitimate security interests' story. Claiming Russia may invade Ukraine because Ukraine wants certain treaties is as preposterous as saying India may invade Bangladesh for signing treaties India dislikes. Sovereignty is black and white.
core_ideas.quote: In my mind, there's a simple line, which is you don't invade your neighbors.

core_ideas.explanation: Putin calls the USSR's collapse a geopolitical tragedy and is rebuilding an empire step by step. He grabs land, sets up fake republics like the DPR and LPR, then arms them in what is passed off as a civil war, which Ajay calls the standard Hitler-Stalin playbook. The underlying idea, the civilizational state, rejects borders altogether: it could justify invading Malaysia to 'protect' ethnic Chinese there.
core_ideas.quote: There is a phrase for it, it's called civilizational state. Okay, the civilizational state is a truly dangerous concept. It is tantamount to the rejection of the basic concepts and discipline of a national border.

core_ideas.concept: Why the invasion failed: ossification and yes-men
core_ideas.explanation: Following Michael Kofman, Amit notes that most people expected the invasion to succeed and the occupation to fail. The surprise was that the invasion itself failed. Big armies, like big companies, ossify and pass information upward slowly. An ageing autocrat with imperial delusions ends up surrounded by yes-men while the best minds disappear into exile, so his delusions go unchallenged.
core_ideas.quote: they get surrounded by yes men. And no one dares to contradict them in any way.

core_ideas.concept: Three levels of governance: why authoritarian militaries are the worst
core_ideas.explanation: Level one is civilian government in a liberal democracy. You don't need the best people inside, because brilliant outside critics find the bugs and propose fixes. Level two is a democracy's military, which is harder because secrecy and patriotism mute criticism, though America's greatness is that its best minds attacked its own Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq wars. Level three is an authoritarian military: critics are silenced, nothing is disclosed and there is no market test. Ajay notes the US publishes how many shells and Javelins it bought each year, while India's budget reveals so little that Japan's military is easier to study. As Amit adds, transparency drives accountability, and accountability drives efficiency. The Indian middle-class instinct that strongmen build strong militaries is backwards.
core_ideas.quote: To understand a state is to understand that authoritarian countries make the worst militaries.

core_ideas.concept: Patriotism is not standing with your government
core_ideas.explanation: Separate the state from the people; a state's actions may not even serve its own people. When your country invades another, rallying around the flag is a basic intellectual blunder. Protest is the patriotic act.
core_ideas.quote: In fact, if our country does something wrong or if our government does something wrong, it is a sign of your patriotism that you protest for the sake of what your country means to you.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay notes that Indian outlets such as Hindustan Times on YouTube swallow Russian propaganda. Amit's diagnosis is that media companies have moved from journalism, with its rigour and pursuit of truth, to a content game of endlessly pumping out 'insight'. In that game the best propaganda machine wins.
core_ideas.quote: it becomes about narrative and not truth

core_ideas.concept: Committed vs involved: morale as a weapon
core_ideas.explanation: In bacon and eggs, the chicken is involved but the pig is committed. Russia fights for one man's grandeur; Ukraine fights for its existence. Ajay adds that war is about money, men, material and morale, and morale can change the whole landscape. It guarantees nothing, though: Austria and Czechoslovakia were still overrun.
core_ideas.quote: the chicken is involved, but the pig is committed.

core_ideas.concept: The revolution in military affairs has arrived
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's history runs in phases: Napoleonic warfare, the stalemate that ended with combined arms in WWI, the interwar integration of tanks and aircraft (Tukhachevsky and German thinkers), a nuclear detour, and the 'RMA' of the 80s and 90s. Ukraine is where that revolution finally plays out, built on two things. The first is near-total battlefield transparency from drones, satellites and electronic monitoring. The second is precision munitions accurate to 10 to 20 metres, versus WWII bombs landing kilometres away. Together they kill WWII doctrine of secretly massing force for a breakthrough.
core_ideas.quote: But think of the footprint that 100 armored fighting vehicles and 1,000 people would leave in the eyes of a satellite. And all you need is 10 artillery shells with cluster munition to make a very bad day for that force.

core_ideas.explanation: Plans collapse on contact with reality. What modern militaries need is the ability to learn, improvise and adapt under fire, which depends on a culture of debate and criticism. Macho, nationalist authoritarian armies lack that culture.
core_ideas.quote: It is to be able to learn, improvise, and adapt under fire. That is state capacity.

core_ideas.concept: Combined arms has a team-size ceiling
core_ideas.explanation: Western combined arms, where infantry, drones, electronic warfare, artillery and tanks act in concert so that 'two and two become twenty-two', needs years of training and life-or-death trust. It is undermined by ordinary human pettiness between specialists. A business rule of thumb says every doubling of headcount demands a redesigned organisation. In practice, Ukraine's hastily trained civilians manage combined arms at about 100 people, and larger operations fumble.
core_ideas.quote: So you can get 100 people to talk to each other and work together. You can't get a thousand people to talk together and work together.

core_ideas.concept: Ukraine is the lab for the next Western way of war
core_ideas.explanation: Western doctrine assumes total air superiority, with the grunts only mopping up. It has never had to deal with skies full of enemy drones, and since WWII it has only fought second- and third-rate opponents. Ukraine is fighting a peer without air superiority. Russia has three times the economy and population, but its incompetence makes the two sides roughly equal. So Ukraine now knows more about conventional war than anyone.
core_ideas.quote: I think that war is the lab where the next generation of the Western way of war is being forged.

core_ideas.concept: Attrition today means deep operations, not 1914
core_ideas.explanation: 'Attritional' brings WWI trenches to mind. Ajay says today's version is Soviet-style deep operations. Using NATO intelligence, partisans and standoff weapons like Storm Shadow and HIMARS, Ukraine destroys ammunition dumps, command posts and supply lines day after day, choking Russia's fuel, food and troop rotation. Fronts like Bakhmut and Zaporizhzhia may be fixing operations. Nobody can tell in advance which will become the breakthrough.
core_ideas.quote: But every attritional war can be a prelude to one side breaking.

core_ideas.concept: Logistics, not the coastline, is the real target
core_ideas.explanation: Crimea's only land link to Russia is the Kerch Bridge, which Ukraine can likely destroy, and the southern front is supplied out of Crimea. Every armchair strategist imagined a 60 to 65 km armoured thrust to the Sea of Azov. The real aim was to cut logistics, such as the M14 highway, which sat beyond HIMARS's roughly 30 km range. Ukraine only needs to creep close enough, with better standoff weapons, to strangle supply.
core_ideas.quote: They've got to get close enough for their standoff weapons to disrupt Russian logistics. And that's not as hard as it seems.

core_ideas.explanation: Americans wanted Ukraine to play like Tal or Fischer, sacrificing material for a crushing breakthrough. Ukraine is playing like Capablanca or Karpov, coordinating patiently and seizing tactical chances only when they appear. It is like Carlsen grinding equal endgames until his opponent cracks, as Nepomniachtchi did in their title match. Bakhmut's effect on Wagner couldn't have been predicted either.
core_ideas.quote: You can never say in advance what is going to break where, but you have to just keep pinging away and something or the other will break.

core_ideas.explanation: Ukraine's real war economy is the combined advanced world: Europe, the US, Japan, South Korea (its top artillery-shell supplier), Australia and Canada. Russia, with a Spain-sized GDP, loses about 1,000 tanks a year while making about 200, and sanctions block any scale-up. So Ukraine can afford to waste equipment but stays frugal with lives. The open question is whether Russia can find Stalin-level resolve in the face of its losses.
core_ideas.quote: once you start thinking that wars are won by economies and not by militaries, then it's clear as day.

core_ideas.concept: Don't assume the mud season ends the fight
core_ideas.explanation: Many expected the rasputitsa, the autumn mud season, to halt the fighting. But the south, around Melitopol, is warmer than Kyiv, hundreds of kilometres away, and the sea moderates the weather. Winter also amplifies Russia's problems with fuel, materials and concealment. The war may well continue into winter, so the 'failed counteroffensive' verdict is premature.
core_ideas.quote: We should not assume that the fighting stops in winter.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: After Amit relays how Gaurav Chintamani was mind-blown by Ajay's five-hour Ukraine masterclass, Ajay deflects: 'I only know 16 things.'
On WWII bombs landing kilometres off target, Amit says: 'So if someone tries to bomb me in Andheri, they'll get you in Bandra.'
After quoting 'The plan is useless. The planning is everything,' Ajay confesses: 'Gentle reader, if ever you think I'm eloquent, I'm actually just a database. I steal stuff.'
Ajay's war math: Russia has three times Ukraine's economy and population, 'And Russian incompetence is like a 0.33 multiplication factor. So the two sides are roughly equal in battle.'
Ajay's one-line verdict on Russia's economy: 'It is Saudi Arabia with nukes.'

Ajay on rivalry between specialists: the drone guy boasts that flying a drone is the greatest skill in the world, and the electronic warfare guy replies, 'Yeah, you guys, you just fly these birds. We, we shoot them down.'
On the dagger thrust to the Sea of Azov, 'dreamt up in public domain by every armchair military strategist in the whole world', Ajay remarks: 'if something is so obvious, you can't be doing that.'
Amit on Tezuka being called both the father and the godfather of manga: 'So father and godfather at the same time.'
Thomas Jefferson's line that liberty requires eternal vigilance, which Amit invokes to argue freedom can't be taken for granted.
Hemingway's For Whom the Bell Tolls and the Spanish Civil War of 1936, Ajay's frame for why a distant war is everyone's business.
Two quotes on plans from Amit: von Moltke's 'no plan survives contact with the enemy' and Mike Tyson's 'Everyone has a plan till they get punched in the face.'

Ulysses S. Grant as the source of the American doctrine of concentrated force. Amit quotes a WWII historian: 'They built a powerful army when the need arose, attacked the enemy's strength as quickly as possible, and took and inflicted casualties until he stopped struggling. Anything less was a distraction.' He also cites Lawrence Freedman's summary of US doctrine as a 'main effort' on a single front.
Marshal Tukhachevsky and the interwar thinkers who worked tanks and aircraft into military doctrine, setting up the Second World War.
Amit's chess pantheon: Capablanca and Karpov as positional masters, Tal and Fischer as attackers, and Kasparov's compliment that Carlsen is a combination of Fischer and Karpov.
Judo, Putin's favourite sport, where the patient, nimble fighter beats the strong one. Amit delights that Ukraine is winning the judo match against Russia.
Putin's own claim that the collapse of the USSR was a great geopolitical tragedy, which Ajay contrasts with his view of it as one of the most glorious moments of the 20th century.
America as the 'arsenal of democracy', the WWII industrial colossus behind both its own way of war and Stalin's strategy.
Gekiga, the dark, adult, urban comics movement Yoshihiro Tatsumi pioneered against cheerier manga. Tatsumi wrote of Tezuka: 'Tezuka was like a god for me.'
